topic: AI hasn’t shifted the bottleneck from coding to code review

# AI Hasn't Shifted the Bottleneck From Coding to Code Review — It Just Made the Old Problem Louder

The pitch from AI coding tool vendors goes something like this: developers are now generating code so fast that code review has become the new constraint. The bottleneck, they claim, has shifted. Teams need new AI-powered review tools to keep up with AI-powered generation.

That story is convenient for selling more tools. It's also not what's actually happening on most teams.

## The Narrative vs. the Reality

There's a persistent claim making the rounds: AI coding assistants have made developers so productive at writing code that review capacity can't keep pace. The logical conclusion, if you believe it, is that teams need to invest in AI code review tools or risk drowning in a backlog of pull requests.

The New Stack recently examined this assumption and found it doesn't hold up under scrutiny. The piece argues that the "bottleneck shift" narrative misunderstands where constraints actually exist in software development — and always have.

Here's the thing: code review was already a bottleneck on many teams before AI assistants showed up. Senior engineers were already overloaded with PR queues. Context switching was already expensive. The human capacity to thoughtfully evaluate someone else's work hasn't changed.

What AI code generation has done is make it easier to produce *more* code. But more code isn't the same as better code. And more code definitely isn't the same as code that's easier to review.

If anything, AI-generated code can be harder to review. It often lacks the idiomatic patterns a human would use. It may be technically correct but structurally unfamiliar. Reviewers have to work harder to understand intent when the person who "wrote" the code didn't actually reason through each line.

## What the Data Actually Shows — Or Doesn't

One challenge in evaluating this trend: the hard data is thin. Vendors promoting AI code review tools have obvious incentives to frame the problem in ways that favor their solutions. Independent measurement of code review velocity across the industry is rare.

What we do have is anecdotal evidence from practitioners. And the pattern I keep hearing doesn't match the vendor narrative.

Teams report that their review bottleneck hasn't gotten worse because of AI coding tools. It's been roughly the same. The constraint was always human attention, and that hasn't changed.

Some teams have seen their PR volume increase — not dramatically, but noticeably. But that increase often comes with quality concerns. More PRs don't automatically mean more shippable features. They sometimes mean more churn, more rework, and more back-and-forth in review comments.

[UNVERIFIED] A few engineering leaders have mentioned that junior developers using AI assistants are submitting PRs earlier in their understanding of a problem, leading to more substantive review feedback and longer review cycles. This would be consistent with the "faster to write, slower to review" dynamic, but I haven't seen published data confirming it.

## Why This Matters for Your Team

If your organization is being sold on the idea that AI has shifted the bottleneck and you need new tools to address it, pump the brakes.

First, diagnose your actual constraint. Is review really where things stall on your team? Or is it design decisions? Environment provisioning? Waiting on stakeholders? Test infrastructure? Many teams assume review is the bottleneck because it's visible — PRs sit in a queue, and everyone can see them. But visible doesn't mean causal.

Second, consider whether adding AI review tools solves the right problem. These tools can catch certain classes of issues: style violations, simple bugs, security patterns they've been trained on. What they can't do — at least not yet — is understand business context, evaluate architectural fit, or make judgment calls about tradeoffs. Those are precisely the things that make code review slow when it's slow.

Third, watch out for the "automation theater" trap. Adding an AI review tool that generates dozens of comments per PR can feel like progress. It looks like review is happening. But if those comments are noise — false positives, obvious suggestions the author would have caught, style nitpicks that don't affect correctness — you haven't reduced the bottleneck. You've added work.

## The Review Problem Was Always About Humans

Let's step back and think about why code review exists in the first place.

It's not just about catching bugs. Good review shares knowledge across a team. It maintains consistency in how problems get solved. It gives senior engineers a chance to mentor junior ones. It creates accountability — someone else looked at this and agreed it was ready.

These functions are fundamentally human. They require understanding intent, not just syntax. They require knowing the history of a codebase and the quirks of the production environment. They require trust between collaborators.

AI tools can assist with the mechanical parts of review. They can flag potential null pointer exceptions or suggest more efficient algorithms. That's valuable. But they can't replace the judgment layer. And the judgment layer is where review actually takes time.

When teams complain about review being slow, they're rarely complaining about how long it takes to spot an obvious bug. They're complaining about the queue — how long it takes before someone with sufficient context and authority even looks at the PR. That's a capacity problem, not a capability problem.

AI hasn't changed this dynamic. Developers were already capable of generating more code than reviewers could absorb. The constraint was always attention. AI just makes it easier to hit that constraint faster.

## The Vendor Incentive Problem

There's an uncomfortable truth in how this narrative gets amplified: the companies claiming AI has shifted the bottleneck are often the same companies selling tools to address the "new" bottleneck.

This isn't necessarily deceptive. These vendors genuinely believe their tools help. And in some cases, they do. But the framing serves their interests in ways that should make you skeptical.

If the bottleneck hasn't actually shifted — if it was always human attention and judgment, and still is — then AI review tools are incremental improvements, not transformational ones. That's a harder sell than "everything has changed and you need our solution."

I'm not saying these tools are worthless. I'm saying the problem definition matters. If you adopt a tool because you believe a bottleneck has shifted when it hasn't, you'll be disappointed when the constraint stays right where it was.

## What About Security Review Specifically?

This is where things get more nuanced, and where I think the honest answer is "it depends."

Security review has some characteristics that make AI assistance more promising:

- **Pattern matching**: Many security vulnerabilities follow recognizable patterns. SQL injection, XSS, hardcoded credentials — these are learnable.
- **Consistency**: Unlike architectural review, security review benefits from rigid consistency. You always want to catch the same classes of issues.
- **Coverage**: Human reviewers miss things. They get tired. They skip files when they're rushed. AI doesn't get tired.

But security review also has characteristics that make AI assistance harder:

- **Context sensitivity**: Whether a pattern is dangerous depends heavily on context. A SQL query constructed from user input is a vulnerability — unless it's been sanitized upstream, or it's in a test file, or the input is from an internal admin-only interface.
- **False positive fatigue**: If an AI tool flags too many non-issues, developers learn to ignore it. This is worse than no tool at all.
- **Novel vulnerabilities**: AI tools can only find patterns they've been trained on. Zero-days and creative attack vectors aren't in the training data.

Teams doing security review — and I include myself here, given my app sec work — need to be realistic about what AI can and can't do. It's a supplement, not a replacement. And it doesn't change the fundamental constraint: someone with security expertise still needs to make judgment calls.

## What to Watch and What to Do Next

### Monitor your actual metrics

Before accepting any narrative about where your bottleneck is, measure it. How long do PRs actually sit in queue? What's the variance? Where do they stall — waiting for initial review, or going through multiple rounds of revision?

If you're using tools like GitHub or GitLab, this data is available. Look at it. Don't assume the bottleneck is where vendors say it is.

### Be skeptical of AI review tools' default configurations

If you do adopt an AI review tool, expect to spend time tuning it. Out-of-the-box configurations tend to be noisy because vendors would rather err on the side of flagging too much than missing something and getting blamed.

Your team will have its own tolerance for what's worth commenting on. Build that into the tool, or your developers will learn to ignore it.

### Invest in reviewer capacity the old-fashioned way

If review really is your bottleneck, the highest-leverage solution might not be technology. It might be:

- Training more people to do effective reviews
- Carving out protected time for senior engineers to focus on review
- Breaking PRs into smaller, more reviewable chunks
- Establishing clearer standards so reviewers don't have to make the same decisions repeatedly

These aren't exciting. They don't involve buying anything. But they address the actual constraint: human attention.

### Watch for second-order effects of AI-generated code

There's a possibility — unproven but plausible — that AI-generated code changes the nature of what review needs to accomplish. If developers are submitting code they understand less deeply, reviewers may need to probe intent more than they used to. That would make review slower, not faster.

Keep an eye on whether your review conversations are changing. Are reviewers asking more "why did you do it this way" questions? That could be a signal.

## The Question No One's Asking

Here's what I keep coming back to: if AI really had shifted the bottleneck, we'd see clear evidence in cycle time data. Teams would be reporting that PRs get written fast but sit in review forever, when that used to be the opposite.

I haven't seen that data. I've seen vendors claiming it must be true, and I've seen practitioners shrugging and saying things look about the same.

Maybe the bottleneck will shift eventually. Maybe as AI coding tools get better — more integrated, more context-aware, more trusted — developers will generate code at rates that genuinely overwhelm review capacity. But that's a future state, not the present.

Right now, the bottleneck looks a lot like it always did: human attention is finite, and there are more things to look at than time to look at them. AI hasn't changed that equation. It's just made it easier to generate more inputs for the same constrained process.

---

**For your team:** Before you buy into the "shifted bottleneck" narrative, ask yourself — has your review capacity actually gotten worse since your team started using AI coding tools? Or did you already have more code than reviewers could handle, and now you just have a vendor telling you it's a new problem?
